The Virginia rail (Rallus limicola) is a secretive marsh bird whose life history reflects the energetic demands of breeding in temperate wetlands. Under the thermal conditions typical of the species' active metabolic period, around 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C], the maximum reproductive rate translates to 4 to 13 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 4 to 13 eggs per clutch] produced over 1 to 2 clutches per year [F_R_i = 1 to 2 clutches per year]. Neonates emerge from eggs that have been incubated for approximately 19 days [ab = approximately 19 days] at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a developmental period consistent with other small rallids. The initial wet weight of a freshly laid egg is recorded at 9.19 grams [Ww0 = 9.19 grams], providing the embryo with substantial yolk reserves to fuel organogenesis within the calcareous shell. These eggs are typically deposited in a well-concealed nest platform woven from cattails and sedges, offering thermal buffering against diurnal temperature fluctuations in the marsh environment.

At the moment of hatching, the wet weight at birth is approximately 5.7 grams [Wwb = approximately 5.7 grams], reflecting the chick's semi-precocial condition. The downy nestling, covered in black natal down, is capable of leaving the nest within hours but remains dependent on parental provisioning for thermoregulation and food delivery. This interval allows for the completion of skeletal growth and the development of the flight musculature necessary for sustained foraging flights across the marsh.

Adults of the Virginia rail exhibit modest sexual size dimorphism in their ultimate body mass. Female ultimate wet weight typically reaches 70 grams [Wwi = 70 grams], with a range of 65 to 77 grams, while the ultimate wet weight of male individuals is approximately 90 grams [Wwi = approximately 90 grams]. This mass difference likely confers advantages to males in territorial defense and courtship displays, particularly during the breeding season when males broadcast their distinctive "kid-ick" calls from elevated perches. The heavier body mass also supports the energetic costs of maintaining a territory in the dense vegetation of freshwater and brackish marshes throughout their breeding range. These values for adult mass were derived from a substantial series of museum specimens and field-captured individuals sampled across the species' distribution from southern Canada to the mid-Atlantic states.

The onset of first reproduction in the Virginia rail is delayed relative to the attainment of puberty, reflecting the need to establish a breeding territory and secure sufficient food resources. The time since birth at first brood is 365 days [tR = 365 days] when measured under the thermal conditions typical of active metabolism at 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C], meaning that most individuals do not breed until their second calendar year. This deferred first breeding is common among rallids and is thought to be linked to the complexity of securing a suitable nesting site within the dynamic marsh environment, where water levels and vegetation density fluctuate annually. Females that breed for the first time in their second year tend to produce smaller clutches, but fecundity increases with age and experience, allowing older females to approach the upper end of the range of 4 to 13 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 4 to 13 eggs per clutch] and up to 2 clutches per year [F_R_i = up to 2 clutches per year].

Longevity records for the Virginia rail remain somewhat sparse, but available data indicate that the maximum lifespan is approximately 8.5 years [am = approximately 8.5 years], a value that must be interpreted cautiously due to the difficulty of tracking individuals across multiple seasons in dense at a temperature of 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C] marsh habitat. This lifespan estimate was recorded under field conditions at 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C], a temperature that approximates the core body temperature during periods of active foraging and territorial defense. The species faces substantial mortality pressure from predators including marsh hawks, mink, and raccoons, as well as from habitat loss, which likely truncates the realized lifespan well below this theoretical maximum. The combination of a moderate lifespan, deferred first reproduction, and relatively small clutch sizes positions the Virginia rail as a K-selected strategist within the Rallidae, investing in adult survival and territory fidelity over maximal annual reproductive output.
